name: Chakhwi
subtitle: Tripuri bamboo shoot stew with raw papaya and a low, savoury note of dried fish

ingredients.note: fermented shoot is traditional; fresh boiled shoot works and is milder
the nearest catalogued stand-in for berma, Tripura's fermented dried fish; toast it hard before use and expect a saltier, cleaner flavour than the original

ingredients.qty: 1 tbsp, slaked in 3 tbsp cold water
ingredients.note: gives the broth just enough body to cling
Tripuri cooking uses very little oil, and the dish is often made with none at all

prepNotes: Toast and crumble the dried fish first, in a separate pan, before anything else goes on the stove.
If your bamboo shoot is fresh, boil it in a change of water for 10 minutes and drain, or the stew will be harsh.
Raw papaya must be genuinely raw and green. A half-ripe one turns to mush and sweetens the pot.

steps.text: Dry-toast the dried fish over low heat for 3 minutes until brittle and strongly fragrant, then crumble it.
Warm the oil in a deep pan and fry the garlic and ginger for 1 minute until they smell sweet.
Add the bamboo shoot and cook 4 minutes, until the sharp raw smell softens.
steps.tip: Do not lean over the pan at this point. Bamboo shoot is aggressive in the first two minutes.

steps.text: Stir in the crumbled fish and the turmeric and cook 1 minute.
Add the papaya, potato and water, bring to a boil, then simmer uncovered 20 minutes until the papaya turns translucent at the edges.
Add the beans and green chillies and simmer 6 minutes more.
Stir in the slaked rice flour and cook 2 minutes, until the broth thickens just enough to leave a film on the spoon.
steps.tip: Slake it in cold water first. Dry flour tipped into hot broth lumps instantly.

steps.text: Season with salt — the dried fish has done much of the work — scatter the coriander and serve with rice.

storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated. The papaya softens further overnight, which most people prefer. Reheat to a bare simmer and loosen with a little water.
